resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
Series and parallel connections are two basic ways to connect conductors.
The quantitative relations below describe steady direct current.
We treat the connecting wires as ideal and neglect their resistance.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**Series connection**
Conductors connected in series are joined end to end, with no current branch in the part of the circuit being studied.
Two conductors with resistances $R_1$ and $R_2$ are connected in series in Figure $173$.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
Here the total resistance is the equivalent resistance of this series part.
It does not include the power source's internal resistance.
Under the same conditions, any number of series conductors has a total resistance equal to the sum of their resistances.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**Parallel connection**
Two conductors with resistances $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in parallel when their ends connect to the same pair of junctions.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before:
Under the same conditions, the sums in formulas (9-8) and (9-9) apply to any number of parallel conductors.
The product-over-sum expression above applies only to two conductors.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**Measuring current**
An ammeter is connected in series with the conductor being measured.
The same current then passes through the ammeter and the conductor, as Figure $175$ shows.

resolvedSectionBreaks.before: The excessive current may burn out the ammeter coil and cause serious danger.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after:
**Measuring voltage**
To measure the voltage across a circuit part of resistance $R$, connect a voltmeter in parallel across its two ends.
